utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, I can hear and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, you may sit down. General Talic, can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED TALIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, I can hear you in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner, Andrew Cayley, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm John Ackerman, I appear with Tanja Radosavljevic and Milan Trbojevic. Good morning to all of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Appearances for General Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I'm Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau representing General Talic with Fabien Masson. And I wish to apologise for my delay because I needed to consult with my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber would have appreciated had you informed Madam Registrar before so that at least we would have utilised the time in our chambers rather than standing here in the corridors not knowing exactly how long it was going to take. But I understand it was an important meeting that you needed to have with your client. And I appreciate that your client is not available much earlier -- much before the sitting is scheduled to start. But please in the future try to avoid having this happening again. Yes. Would you like to say something, General Talic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED TALIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I would like my defence not to proceed in this way, and I wish to change my attorney. I should like to talk to attorney Slobodan Zecevic for Natasha to remain in the team for the trial to continue with Ms. Natasha Fauveau conducting the proceedings until the formalities are completed over attorney Zecevic. Mr. De Roux would remain as a consultant in the Defence team. Thank you, Your Honour, for hearing me out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you, General Talic. Have you informed and have you started the -- your discussions with the office -- with the office of this Tribunal that these -- with this matter -- with these matters?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED TALIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately I have not, but I will do so during the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau. You may sit down, General Talic. Please feel free to express your concerns on these matters with the Trial Chamber at any time. And you will have the support and the help of the Trial Chamber in making sure that you are adequately represented in this -- in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED TALIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want you to know, both of you -- both Mr. Brdjanin and yourself -- that your interests are the interests of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED TALIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is quite clear to me, and I hope so too for Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should simply like to say that I will do everything I can to speed up the procedure, and I will contact Mr. Zecevic immediately after today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is Mr. Zecevic -- and forgive me if I am not pronouncing his name well -- present here in The Hague, or is he somewhere else and needs to be contacted?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He's in Belgrade just now. But I think he's ready to come as quickly as possible in a very short time, anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That concludes the part on General Talic. One moment, Ms. Korner. Mr. Ackerman, I have been handed an official confirmation that Mr. Trbojevic has been appointed co-counsel. I do notice that the form adopted and the words adopted by the office in this particular appointment are somewhat different, that they have -- than they have been in the past. I would like you to come forward as soon as practicable with the confirmation that I had asked of you when Ms. Radosavljevic -- Madam Radosavljevic was appointed co-counsel temporarily, asking you to make the same declaration with regard to your new co-counsel, because it's important for this Tribunal to know that at any time you are not in a position to be present, that he can take over and continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I can just say, Your Honour, that he has been working very hard trying to get caught up with the -- what has happened so far in the case. He's been going through the exhibits, going through a lot of the witness statements, things like that. He can't, of course, go through the transcripts, because they're not available in B/C/S, and we're trying to figure out a way to bring him up to date with regard to those and will. But I think he will be fully participating in this case by the end of this week, if not early part of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a couple of matters to raise this morning, one which is going to take a little bit of time. But on what's just been said by General Talic -- because obviously it affects witnesses. Do I understand this, that the gentleman from Serbia -- well, first of all, he has to be appointed by the Registry -- will be taking over as lead counsel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I -- that's how I have understood it. But I don't know. Maybe General Talic would like to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED TALIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He will be lead counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I understood it. Yes. Thank you, General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's -- you see, this is what's going to maybe cause a problem. And I really raise it now for the time being just so that it's mentioned. As Mr. Ackerman has just said in respect of Mr. Trbojevic, it's going to take some time, particularly for someone who doesn't read English or French --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- To catch up with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are assuming that he doesn't. I mean, I'm not making that assumption. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there'll be no problem. Mr. Zecevic speaks English perfectly. He was involved in another case. So I don't think he will have any problems. In fact, I've already spoken to the Registry, and I don't think there will be any problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry for interrupting you the way I did, Ms. Korner. But --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It saves time, Your Honour, if that's right, if he speaks some -- fluent English. Your Honour, may I raise then the two matters. One is a short and fairly simple one, I hope. I received a letter from Madam Fauveau in which she stated that on behalf of General Talic, there was -- they did not contest the fact of the killings in the village of Skrljevita. That's the one that Kajtez was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And indeed that at least one of the perpetrators was a member of the Army of the Republika Srpska. And there are various caveats, but they needn't -- Your Honours needn't worry about them at this stage. All that I want to know is -- because this witness, the witness who's due to testify to these events, is due to arrive next week to testify. And I've asked Madam Fauveau whether in those circumstances, the statement can be read. I notice there's no -- there's no way apparently in the Rules of reading a statement without getting a Rule 92 declaration. But that can be achieved, I hope, without too much difficulty at some stage. But I need to have an answer this week so we don't bring the witness here unnecessarily. And I'm taking it from Mr. Ackerman's comments last time a witness came where there was no dispute as to the killing that he takes the same line as Madam Fauveau; in other words, that there's no dispute. But I need to raise that now, so that I need an answer about this particular witness, who is Witness 7.76 -- whether that statement can be read. So I raise that now.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask Madam Korner whether I could give my answer tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I -- I don't know whether Mr. Ackerman has got any comments on this particular ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I had filed a letter saying that I do not contest the -- the actual killings themselves, that the people were in fact killed. That's still my position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I need to know whether I need to call the witness at all or whether that statement will be accepted or read under --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the point --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- Rule 92.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the point being made by Ms. Korner, actually. It's not whether you still contest or not contest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have no desire to see the witness. The statement is fine for me. But it really affects -- it doesn't affect us. It really affects General Talic. So I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It shouldn't turn on the way I feel about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's the second matter I have to turn to is I'm afraid going to take a little longer. And that's -- it relates to the cross-examination last week of Judge Draganovic. Your Honour, I think I should preface what I have to say by, I think, reminding all of us that these proceedings are being held in an international arena and they're being widely publicised, particularly in the territories of the former Yugoslavia. Your Honour, it's my understanding and belief and, if you like, training, that counsel in particular are under a duty to behave with propriety and to ensure that allegations which could be described as those being of a scandalous nature in the widest form of the word are not made without due consideration and reflection and most importantly without some proper foundation for making such an allegation, whether it's from reliable evidence or from instructions, but above all it should, we submit, have some relevance to the issues in the case and not merely be, if I can put it that way, a scatter-gun approach which is designed to really throw a lot of mud. Now, Your Honour, the witnesses who appear here in trials of these sort -- and it doesn't matter whether they're trials of alleged Croat perpetrators or Serb or Muslim. Nearly all of the witnesses will fall into the category in some aspect or another of that of a victim. And Your Honour, the Statute recognise that, because in Article 22 it's stated that: "The International Tribunal shall provide in its Rules of Procedure and Evidence for the protection of victims and witnesses such protection measures shall include but shall not be limited to" -- and I emphasise that -- "the conduct of in camera proceedings and the protections of victim's identities." Your Honour, in Rule 75 it's stated that -- this is Rule 75(C): "A Chamber shall whenever necessary control the manner of questioning to avoid any harassment or intimidation." Your Honours, in fact -- or Your Honour, the opening remarks that you made before the case was opened on the 23rd of January in the transcript at page 679 in fact set out, as it were, the rules that you wished counsel and others to follow in this trial. And clearly Your Honour had in mind the code of conduct that has been drafted for Defence counsel, because when I looked at that, it was quite clear that parts had been quoted. And I include -- Your Honour, this is page 679, line 22. "We'll be on the watch out for something which is fundamental -- fundamentally important for the proper conduct of the proceedings, namely that you are never expected to make an incorrect statement of material fact or offer evidence which you know to be correct." And then you dealt with the integrity of evidence. And then: "Dealing with cross-examination, I expect both -- I expect you, both the Prosecution and the Defence, again, to show the utmost courtesy towards witnesses both in examination-in-chief as well as -- as well as in cross-examination. You are, of course, free to examine and cross-examine witnesses to the best of your ability and in the way you deem fit and proper and also considering the attitude that each witness takes in any particular moment. But dealing adequately with the witness is one thing; failing to show courtesy or resorting to practices which will not be acceptable to this Tribunal, such as undue aggressiveness towards the witness, will not be allowed." Now, Your Honour, the witness who was here for the last two weeks was in fact a victim as well as someone who was giving evidence of his investigations. And Your Honour, he's someone, we would submit, who by virtue of his position is someone particularly in Bosnia who's in the public eye. And such a person will suffer more than the ordinary person -- although, of course, it's -- it's not to decry or lessen the effect allegations of misconduct will have on the ordinary witness, but it's far more serious, we would submit, when those allegations are made against someone in his position, because obviously very much the situation will apply that there's no smoke without fire. And so Your Honour, our submission is -- and that's why I'm raising it, because there are a number of witnesses who Your Honours are going to hear from who do hold positions of responsibility and in the public eye in Bosnia who are to come -- that care should be taken before making allegations. Now, Your Honour, I can just summarise the effect of the evidence that Judge Draganovic gave. He gave evidence of fact, the build-up of the -- to the events in -- leading up to the takeover in Sanski Most; his arrest and subsequent incarceration in the police station, the SUP, and Manjaca, and what happened to him; and then his subsequent investigations, the exhumations, the discovery of documents, and his collaboration with the Bosnian government agency known as AID. And that was in connection with the submission of documents to this Tribunal. Now, Your Honour, it's absolutely right that from the beginning of this case the Defence have made it clear that they challenge the authenticity of documents which have not been stamped or signed. Mr. Ackerman on the 4th of February, at page 1385 of the transcript, went a little further, saying that he was -- his words were: "We are concerned about the source of some of the documents, even though there's an identified source, because we are not convinced that the source is reliable. For example, for a source which is adversarial to our clients." Now, Your Honour, in respect of Sanski Most, we were given a list by Madam Fauveau of documents to which objection was taken. But obviously because of Your Honours' ruling, just so that it was noted, I do not recall being given any such list by Mr. Ackerman but I may be wrong about that. Now, Your Honour, I make it absolutely clear: The Prosecution fully understands, appreciates, and shoulders its burden which is to satisfy Your Honours that documents which have been admitted into evidence are reliable. But equally, Your Honour, we would expect that Defence counsel, particularly in the interests of a speedier trial for the accused would indicate which documents outside those that are obvious - no stamp, no signature - are seriously contested or alleged to be forgeries. Your Honour, in respect of General Talic, we have no complaints about the cross-examination at all. It was effectively a testing of the evidence in respect of Manjaca. There was questioning about the map, you will recall, Bosanski Brod, and the routes that were taken. And Your Honour -- but the way -- the form of the questioning, we submit, was a proper one, because it wasn't an assertion -- because they couldn't make that assertion because they had no evidence that these were forgeries -- but the question was put: "Would you allow for the possibility that the map was not made by members of the 6th Brigade?" So the issue is clear. And we understand that we have to show Your Honours that this map is authentic. The same with Rasula's diary, in respect -- which affects General Talic directly because of the record of the meeting. It was -- he was -- the witness was cross-examined on the basis that some of the words were in Latin script, and the question was properly put: "Would you accept that someone might have been able to add some words to that diary before it was found," and so on and so forth. Your Honour, the questioning when it came on behalf of Mr. Brdjanin was very different. Your Honour, the matters began with an attempt to enter into evidence a transcript of evidence in another case relating to the statement of a witness not before the Court. And Your Honours haven't, in fact, ruled upon that, but Your Honours have heard the objection. Your Honour, then a series of names were put to the judge. And this is at page 5912 of the transcript. When Mr. Ackerman was invited by me -- and Your Honours accepted the invitation -- to explain that list of names, the explanation he gave, in the absence of the witness but in open court -- and I emphasise that -- was apparently that that list of names were a list of people who worked for AID, one of whom was the ex-head of AID. The allegation made -- and Your Honour, I think it maybe as well if I -- if I just remind Your Honour of what was actually said. Your Honour -- I'm sorry. Again, this is page 5915. "Your Honour, I can tell you only my current understanding, and I can also tell you this matter is -- continues to be under investigation. But it is clear that five individuals have been arrested and are sitting in jail in Sarajevo, having been detained on the orders of Judge Putica. They are described as five former officials of AID and their associates. They are charged by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina with engaging in terrorist activities with manufacturing documents. It's a very, very serious matter. There is an article about it in Oslobodenje, and I've -- and I have an investigation going on trying to find out more about it. They apparently also were engaged in some kind of a plot to assassinate Fikret Abdic." Now, Your Honour, first of all, the implication that the Trial Chamber must be being asked to draw is that the -- these officials of AID -- and taking it a step further -- AID generally were involved in forgery of documents and that because in the investigative capacity as a judge, the witness collaborated with AID, therefore he is in some way tainted or less likely to be believed. Now, Your Honour, the submission we make is this, that if allegations about a government agency are to be made in this forum, counsel surely have a duty to make all possible checks and make sure that the information is accurate. Now, Your Honour, as a result of it being raised, we are in the process of making full inquiries as to what the situation is. And -- yes, I'm quite -- I'm grateful. I read out -- this is the way it's come out in the transcript. It's absolutely right. Mr. Ackerman said, "Slobodna Bosna." I was quite surprised when I saw the words "Oslobodjenje." But Your Honour, we're making -- and if necessary, we can and will put evidence before the Court about what is involved. But Your Honour, it's important in our submission to give the Trial Chamber at least what we understand to be the accurate account at the moment of what this concerns. Your Honour, it -- indeed one of the many inquiries that could have been made was to contact the newspaper itself and perhaps speak to the editor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for one moment, Ms. Korner. Madam Registrar, we have a witness awaiting outside presumably in a room. Make sure that he is looked after and that someone explains to him why he is being kept there and not giving evidence here. Could you make -- take the necessary next steps, please. Sorry, Ms. Korner. But --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour is quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want to make sure that this gentleman is -- knows that there's nothing happening that relates to him or that he should be worrying about or that we are just being oblivious of his presence here. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm grateful for that. Your Honour, our understanding from the checks that we were able to make over the Friday and the weekend is as follows, that as listed in this newspaper, the ex-head of AID has been arrested with four other people. The charges apparently relate to operations allegedly - and I emphasise this because all of this at the moment is mere charges - carried out against the gentlemen Fikret Abdic that Mr. Ackerman explained to you who he was, in the period 1995 to 1996. The charges in relation to forgery is levelled exclusively against the ex-head, Mr. Alispahic, and it relates to identification papers given to persons who had attended some kind of military training camp. It's called camp Pogorelica again in 1995 to 1996. Now, Your Honour, it may well be that at some stage by calling proper evidence the Defence may wish to persuade Your Honours that these events do cast out upon the authenticity of the documents that have been supplied by AID. Your Honour, one of the many tasks that we are going to be undertaking is to show that the content of those documents can be supported by evidence, in other words, by witnesses. But Your Honour, our submission is the manner in which that was introduced last Thursday is in fact improper. Your Honour, there is no link that the Defence are able to demonstrate or could at the time that they put these questions with this witness. There's no evidence at all to show that he was in any way connected with any of those events which are way outside the ambit of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, if I'm not mistaken, having come -- having concluded that series of questions, Mr. Ackerman himself conceded that and did not proceed any further. So I don't think it's the case of hammering it in -- out because I think there is -- the triangle is perfect.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, our submission is it should never have been dealt with in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How can you expect counsel to establish whether there has been a contact or not or a connection or not without putting the questions? At least whether he knew -- he knew these persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, my -- the complaint that we make is he could have been asked whether he knew these persons without there being any description of why he was being asked that. That would have been the proper way to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You brought up --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: She asked me to describe why I was asking it. That's why there was a description. She asked for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I said I'm going to do it in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman I did not give you permission to stand up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, we decided to ask the witness to leave the courtroom and inquire what this was all about because you raised the objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know I did, Your Honour. But that doesn't allow Mr. Ackerman -- Mr. Ackerman has no evidence to suggest there's any connection. There is his description of the charges was in our submission misleading because it led Your Honour to believe that there was some connection with the documents in this case. And as far as we understand, there's no connection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. It did not lead the Chamber to believe that. It made the suggestion --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which could be as wide as you can imagine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely. And Your Honour, that's our submission. That is improper in the way this has been raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not necessarily. Depends.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm -- I see that Your Honour -- I'm raising these matters now because they do concern us. Your Honour, that's the first matter. The witness was then accused of effectively being involved in the theft of a roof in order to rebuild his own house. That's at page 5931. Your Honour, then this exceedingly curious allegation that on one of the three statements taken from potential witnesses, his signature had been forged -- not that he forged it, but that his signature had been forged. And the way it was put, Your Honour -- and this again is the complaint that I make about this -- is the manner in which allegations are put. Your Honour, he was asked to look at the three signatures in blown-up form. And it was put at page 6009. "Now, sir, there are three different signatures there, all of which you have told us are yours. Which of those are not yours?" "All three are my signature." And then we heard handwriting evidence from Mr. Ackerman? "Look at the one on the bottom, sir. You don't make an L like that, an L at the end of Adil. And you don't make a C like that at the end of Draganovic. That is clearly written by someone else, isn't it?" Now, Your Honour, is it my understanding of the rule is that is why you have expert handwriting evidence because counsel are not experts in handwriting. The assertion was made in that form that there was no doubt -- because counsel believed it to be so -- that those were forged signatures. Mr. Ackerman later told Your Honour that he had no evidence in his possession at all to suggest that one of those signatures was not the judge's, other than his own supposition. Your Honour -- and I ask to what issue does that form of cross-examination go? Your Honour indeed yourself said at the end that you didn't understand to what issue it went. Your Honour, it is not suggested that he forged his own signature or forged someone else's signature, and it's not clear whether it's suggested that forgery was done with or without his own knowledge. Your Honour, finally, we have the lengthy trawl through the documents relating to the witness's civil suit against Rasula and others. On the basis that it was put to him -- I'm not sure on what possible basis evidentially -- but if the Chamber were to find that he was telling the truth about Mahala, that would help him in a civil suit; that throughout his testimony he had gratuitously volunteered that there had been no resistance in Mahala. Your Honours, we did a check over the transcript over the weekend, and it's right to say there were precisely three references, each time in respect of actual questions, either by myself or Mr. Ackerman. And then, Your Honour, in cross -- and then the basis for suggesting this was then dealt with at page 6028 of the transcript. Your Honour, we were dealt when I asked for an explanation for this: "In the face of this evidence to the contrary and throughout the testimony, even when not asked, this judge has gratuitously thrown in that there was no fighting in Mahala, that nobody was armed and nobody had weapons." And Your Honour: "A finding by this Tribunal that there was no fighting in Mahala could be used by him" -- and I emphasise the following words -- "I think" -- in his lawsuit... Now, Your Honour, it is the cardinal rule of all Bar Associations, I imagine, in the world that what counsel thinks is irrelevant -- counsel may think what he likes, but the question is, "Is there evidence or some basis for making these suggestions?" And Your Honour, then we dealt with the other allegations that were made. And Mr. Ackerman said this in response to a question from you. "Mr. Ackerman, are you suggesting that the witness -- are you suggesting that the witness lied to the Trial Chamber when he said there was no resistance, no fighting in Mahala?" I'm suggesting that it's highly probable that he did, because of the lawsuit that he has. It's worth 100.000 Deutschemarks to him. That's what I'm suggesting." Your Honours said: "In my mind, it's all tied up." And he said: "I don't know that he lied. I wasn't there. But I'm suggesting that it's highly probable that I did. I'm also suggesting that it's highly probable that one of those signatures that we saw today is not his. Just looking at it, anyone would conclude that one of those signatures can't be his, because it's written very different. It's a completely different handwriting. Now, whether I'm right about that or not, it's going to depend, I suppose, on a handwriting expert looking at it and giving us an opinion." Your Honour, in our submission, that should have been done first, not the allegation put in the way it was. Your Honour, the allegation could have been put, "Are you sure that you signed all those three signatures?" And thereafter, he could have been asked to provide samples. Mr. Ackerman then went on: "Whether that turns out -- if my suspicion about that is correct or not, I don't know. But I'm not a handwriting expert" - quite - "so I can't make that conclusion." And then finally Your Honour asked: "Are you suggesting that as regards to proceedings in Sanski Most or whatever, where the judge Edina was presiding, he manipulated the situation? Are you making that suggestion?" "I have no basis upon which to make that, but I think it's highly probable." And then he gave Your Honour an explanation about no country in the world. Now, Your Honour, it is -- and I return to what I said in the beginning. Your Honour, it is incumbent in this trial even more than in any other ordinary trial for counsel, as I say, to behave with propriety and to make suggestions of a scandalous nature as these were in respect to this man with some care before making them. Your Honour, of course Defence counsel have a duty to represent their clients to the best of their ability and to put matters which are helpful to their client's case, but Your Honour they equally do have a duty in our submission -- and it applies to the Prosecution as much as the Defence when we get to the Defence case -- to act responsibly and to act with care before making such allegations. And Your Honour, we really do say that it's not for the Prosecution to protect its own witnesses or the witnesses it's called. Your Honours are there presiding. Your Honours, we would submit respectfully, do have a duty to stop and prevent cross-examination which goes, we submit, beyond the bounds of what is acceptable. And Your Honour the way that those matters were put to Judge Draganovic last week, we submit, was an improper way of cross-examining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. I can assure you that the Chamber did take into consideration most of what you have stated, while Mr. Ackerman was conducting his cross-examination and that it gave due weight to these considerations when it decided not to stop Mr. Ackerman from putting and continuing with the questions he was putting at the time. And as an ex-Defence counsel, I would tell you straight away -- and I'm sure that you have that experience as well -- that the way the Defence counsel conducts his cross-examination is his own business and he is bound to stop -- he has a responsibility stop to stop when he is asked to stop. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I -- I would prefer not to use up a bunch of time to respond to anything that the Chamber is not interested in hearing my response to. So if there are matters that you want me to respond to, I'd be happy to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not particularly, Mr. Ackerman. Not particularly. I can assure everyone present here and everyone who is not present here that last Friday's sitting was a difficult sitting, not just for Mr. -- for Judge Draganovic. It was a much more difficult sitting for us three sitting here, because we had to make assessments as the situation enveloped and -- we had to take some serious decisions. But the situation is that it was the -- the decision that we took was the decision which was the right one. Given the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't -- I can't say any more. I've made the position quite clear, and if Your Honour takes that view --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But Ms. Korner, I can assure you that had you been sitting in my place last Friday, you would have probably come to the same conclusion as we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't think it's right for me to speculate on what I would have done. I merely put the position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I am speculating, not you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should say -- and that's the -- I meant to say that. But also, I think, and I reflected on it afterwards, I think that perhaps the propriety that I'm complaining about equally applies to the criticism that could have been made to some of the remarks that I made. And if I may, I wish to apologise to the Chamber for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not necessary, Ms. Korner. But what I do want to make clear, that any witness that comes to give evidence here will be treated like every other witness. And the higher the position that witness occupies, the more careful you have to be in bringing him forward and he has to be in -- or she has to be in providing the answers, particularly if it's a witness who has never heard of the saying that people who live in glass houses ought not to throw stones. I can assure you that a judge, politician, a lawyer, a Dr. -- you only make one mistake in your life, one mistake, and it can haunt you all -- throughout the rest of your life. And if that mistake is known, it will be thrown at you the moment you sit down there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I think Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Irrespective of whether it is a mistake or not. But it's a question of -- the moment you decide to accept to come forward as a witness, you have to be prepared to answer all the questions that are put to you, that are allowed by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it seems to me that there's one overriding principle, and that is, the matters about which the questioning is allowed relevant to the matters about which he has given evidence. And the lovely catchall phrase that it goes to the credibility of the witness, it's only relevant that the witness's credibility -- if the evidence he's given is in some way disputed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour can I say this just in relation to Mahala. Your Honour, there is ample evidence available undoubtedly to the Prosecution about what actually happened from people who were there. Your Honours are going to be hearing from other people who were present when the attack on Mahala took place. So it's then for Your Honour to judge, having heard that evidence, whether the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- The suggestions made -- and that's what I mean, Your Honour. The suggestions were all dressed up on the basis that Your Honours would treat his evidence about Mahala differently having heard all the other matters that were put. Well, Your Honours are going to hear that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I can assure you, Ms. Korner that, we keep our eyes wide open. You will never catch us asleep for just one single minute. And with regard to the Mahala incident, I can assure you that I had gone through the documentation that Mr. Ackerman had sought to bring in evidence regarding -- to the original motion that Judge Draganovic filed in the Sanski Most court, in which he makes a clear allegation as to what were the circumstances when -- during which his house was burnt down or destroyed. And again, that's something that you don't know, because you wouldn't know what -- what we know. But that's something that we take into consideration the moment we allow the question. Now, whether we believe Mr. Ackerman or whether -- believe Mr. Ackerman -- give weight to Mr. Ackerman's allegation or to the witness of Judge Draganovic, that's another -- that's another question. You will only know that when we come to the final judgement, if we need to spell that out. But until -- until then, just -- the situation is that fortunately we come prepared. None of us three comes here not knowing exactly what the witness has stated beforehand or what is contained in the documents that are brought forward. It's unfortunate that sometimes documents come at the last minute and we don't have that much time to read them before they are put to the witness, but we don't read them before; we read them immediately after or during the break. So I can assure you, Ms. Korner, that it -- last Friday's silent decisions --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thursday. Sorry. Last Thursday's silent decisions that we were making and taking from time to time were suffered decisions, but we needed to take those decisions as taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, there's nothing more I can say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Ackerman, I don't think you need to explain anything. I mean, it's -- if at any time the Chamber believed that you were overstepping what anyone of us three would have done in your place, given the information, we would have stopped you, as we will in future when you overstep.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I expect you will, Your Honour. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we bring in the witness. I understand, Mr. Cayley, you are taking over now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Korner --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood this morning that there was a witness statement that was not disclosed to me. Apparently it was sent to my office in Paris with an explanation that it would be put in my mail box here in the Tribunal. So it was never put there, and actually I saw it five minutes before the beginning of this morning's business. And my assistant left yesterday to look for it in Paris. Therefore, I will need at least a half an hour to consult with my client regarding that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is this -- are we -- may I ask you, Madam Fauveau, whether you are referring to the statement that we found on our desk this morning as well by the witness, dated 23rd May 2002? Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's -- I think it's apparent from the statements, the corrected statements, the witness went through his original statement. It's a page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Where he's gone through the original statement he made and said there are some mistakes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I have a practical solution. We will break now rather than in a quarter of an hour's time. We will have the usual break of 30 minutes, during which time I suppose you will have enough time to read this extra page and also make consultations with your client if needs be.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. That is a solution that would suit me very much. But I would like to draw the attention of the Prosecution to communicate documents to me here in The Hague, because that is where I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: My apologies. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, that applies to you as well, to make sure --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It what does, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau's -- Madam Fauveau's request that in future all documents be forwarded to her in her office here and not in Paris.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we act as one on the Prosecution. So I take it that when the Prosecution is mentioned, that applies to me, Mr. Cayley, and anybody else on the team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. No. But I knew that you did not have the phones and I didn't know whether you were following or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So 30 minutes. We will resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just for the purposes of the regard, Ms. Korner is no longer in the courtroom. And they're proceeding to get the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The usher?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. I suppose he has already gone to bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, General Talic, during the break, have you been contacted or did you try to contact anyone with regard to the appointment and nomination of the lead counsel? I suppose I see Ms. -- Madam Fauveau on her feet. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I contacted Mr. Rhodes [As interpreted] immediately, and he told me that there would be no problem. So I have a meeting with Mr. Rhodes [As interpreted] this afternoon after the hearing, and I shall try to contact Mr. Zecevic immediately too, unless Mr. Rhodes [As interpreted] does that before me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think that's satisfactory. However, if at any time you see that you are being neglected or you're not being given all due attention, please do bring that to our attention immediately.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED TALIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. It's quite clear to me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, just for -- Oh, I'm sorry. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: For the purposes of planning, this witness will go into tomorrow. I don't think he's going to be as lengthy as Draganovic. Simply -- I don't -- I don't want to sort of repeat much of the evidence that's been given. But he certainly will go into tomorrow. And I've allowed a day for cross-examination, although of course if it goes on longer than that, that's a matter for the Defence. The next witness available to testify will be on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness, please. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I was just going to point out that the transcript discloses that Ms. Fauveau talked with Mr. Rhodes. And I think she said Mr. Rohde, who is the person that I'm sure she talked to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. According to the Rules, before you start giving evidence, you are required to make a solemn declaration to tell us the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The usher will hand you the document which contain this statement which you are kindly asked to read out aloud. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I notice that you are a lawyer by profession, and therefore that spurs me having to explain the set-up in this Tribunal. As you can figure out, we are the three Judges dealing with this case. To your right, the gentleman standing and who will commence the examination-in-chief very shortly is the Prosecutor. And to your left, you see two rows. In the front row, you have the Defence team for Radoslav Brdjanin, and in the back row you have the Defence team representing General Momir Talic. Later on you will have a more direct encounter with the gentleman and the lady in these two rows when they proceed with -- when they come to the cross-examination. But for the time being, you are going to be asked questions by the Prosecution in chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, your name is Mirzet Karabeg; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you were born on the 20th of December, 1943 in Sanski Most; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you are of Bosniak nationality; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you are of Islamic or Muslim faith; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the Judge has already stated to you that the Court knows that you are a lawyer by profession. Am I right in saying that you studied law in Zagreb and Sarajevo and completed your legal studies in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You practiced law, I think, from 1975 to 1982; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes. In the administrative bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think from 1982 you were the head of personnel or human resources at the Famos factory in Sanski Most; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, correct. The Famos factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's move straight to 1990. And if you can think about that year. You were a candidate for the SDA party in Sanski Most in the year 1990; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: It is. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think after the 1990 elections, you were appointed as the president of the executive board of Sanski Most. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Municipality of Sanski Most. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you held that position from the 1st of January of 1991 until the 17th of April of 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the president of the executive board of the municipality, is that the second most important political position within the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What is the foremost position in the municipal government?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: The president of the municipality -- excuse me. In the government. President of the government -- the president of the executive board.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the president of the executive board is in effect the head of the executive branch of the local government, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of the executive branch of the local authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the other position that you mentioned, the president of the municipality -- the president of the municipal assembly is the head of the legislature. Is that broadly correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: It is. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was your function as the president of the executive board in relation to the president of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, the implementation, execution of the decisions and other acts and what had been agreed upon on the level of the municipality of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So it was your function to implement the decisions that were decided upon in the municipal assembly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, before we get to the meat of your testimony, I want to move forward in time. You left the municipality of Sanski Most in August of 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes. It was on the 28th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And after that departure, you spent some time in the Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And we'll deal with that later in your testimony. After you left the Manjaca camp, where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: After leaving the Manjaca camp, I was exchanged and I left for Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And in 1992/1993, Travnik was in Bosnian government-controlled territory; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What did you do in Travnik after you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: After arriving to Travnik, we set up the presidency of the Crisis Staff for Sanski Most in exile, and then we set it up in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you tell the Judges a little bit about your post-war political career. So after 1995 and your return to Sanski Most. Could you tell them about your political career.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: After the liberation of Sanski Most, we -- it was important -- the War Presidency of Sanski Most was appointed by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the 13th of March, 1996, the temporary -- the interim assembly was set up of the deputies elected in 1992 and which was active up to the first elections held in the post-war period in Bosnia and Herzegovina. After that from November 1996 I was elected in the cantonal government of Una and Sana for -- as a justice minister and minister for administrative and governmental issues. After a two-year term and its expiry, I was elected for -- a cantonal minister for social issues, for refugees, and displaced persons and -- which I occupied till 1999, after which the term expired. From the 1st of January 2000, I opened my office as a lawyer. And this is what I have been active in since then till the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karabeg. If we can now go back to January of 1991. The municipal assembly in Sanski Most, I'm right in saying, was split between the SDS, the SDA, and the HDZ; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think the -- please continue.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: And there were deputies from -- SDP from the Reform forces, the so-called block of the left forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No one party had an absolute majority, did they, in the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No, they had not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think I'm right in saying the SDS had 23 seats, the SDA 22 seats, the HDZ 4 seats, and the other parties you referred to had 11 seats. Does that sound about right to you?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, 11 -- yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, is your witness still a member of the House of Representatives in the Federal parliament in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think not, Your Honour. He's a lawyer in private practice. But we can ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Are you still a member of the House of Representatives in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was for two -- for two terms I was in the parliament, in the House of Representatives. But I'm not any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In 1991, who was the president of the municipal assembly in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Nedeljko Rasula.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And he was a member of the SDS party; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, very briefly, in the first few months after the 1990 elections, how did the political institutions function in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Very well. We were happy. The Communist system was toppled, and we cooperated in the most excellent manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, since Mr. Rasula was the president of the assembly and you were the president of the executive board, did you meet on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, we did. Every morning we'd begin working at 7.00 a.m., and we would meet between 7.00 and 8.00, have coffee, and discuss the activities of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: During that time, how would you describe your relationship with Mr. Rasula?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Correct. A correct relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, let's move forward in time. And if you can direct your mind to March of 1991. Now, in March of 1991, you attended a meeting in Banja Luka as the president of the executive board of Sanski Most. Do you recall that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I do remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you describe to the Judges why that meeting was convened, who was there, and what was said.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, in Banja Luka in the conference room of the Banja Luka municipality building, the president of the municipality and the presidents of the executive boards of 17 Krajina municipalities were invited to attend. The composition was on the basis of the elections in 90 per cent of the municipalities you had 90 per cent of representatives of the Serbian nation, both in the legislative and the executive branches. I came to that meeting. I found the invitation waiting for me on the table. I went and I met a friend, also a Bosniak, Asim Medaric [phoen], who was the head of the -- the president of the executive board of the municipality of Kljuc. At the meeting what was put forward -- the question was raised, what do balijas and Ustashas want? That was the jargon being used. Many other things were also said. During the break, the two of us commented. We said, "My goodness. How did we end up here?" And we were stunned to hear this being said at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karabeg, just to clarify. You said "during the break, the two of us commented 'my goodness, how did we end up here'?" Who were you referring to? Your Honours and who else?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Asim Medaric, who was the president of the executive board of the municipality of Kljuc. That is the person I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, just from your recollection how many Bosniak Muslims were present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Only the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the other delegates that were present were Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. The other -- I would have known the other Bosniaks, namely Muhamed Cehajic -- the late Muhamed Cehajic, who was the president of the municipality of Prijedor at the time. But a few days later I asked him why he -- didn't he attend that meeting, and he answered that he didn't receive the invitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you've said in your evidence that at the meeting, what was put forward -- the question was raised what to do with the balijas and Ustashas want. That was the jargon being used. Can you remember now after all these years anything specific that was said about the balijas and the Ustashas at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, they -- it was said that the numbers of balijas and Ustashas should be reduced. That means should be assured for the Serbian Krajina -- later the region -- later the Republika Srpska, that there -- many media of the balija and the Ustasha -- this referred to the Bosniak and Croatian televisions; and that all means should be used in order to prevent it from these media being seen and heard on this territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, after hearing these comments -- actually, the first question I have for you is: Do you recall who said this? If you don't, simply say you can't remember. But do you recall who made these comments about balijas and Ustasha?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I do not recall any of the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Having --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Neither did I know these names at the time, because the people who were intervening did not introduce themselves. But as I have mentioned, it was a meeting of the presidents of the municipalities and of the executive boards of the 17 municipalities of the Bosnian Krajina of the Banja Luka region.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you've already stated that you spoke with your Bosniak colleague about what had been stated. Did you address any of your concerns about what you'd heard to any of the Serb delegates that were at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: And how. We had the break. We had breakfast there, had kebab, and then we returned in order to hear what was being discussed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Specifically what I'm asking you is whether or not you addressed any of your concerns about what you'd heard to any of the Serb delegates. If the answer to that question is no, can you state why you didn't address any of your concerns.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: At the meeting itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, it would have no purpose. Maybe they would laugh at this concern of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you stay for the whole meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And do you recall approximately when it ended?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: That meeting ended approximately -- it could have ended at about 2.00 p.m. It began at 11.00, and then there was a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And then at 2.00, am I right in saying you returned to Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was Mr. Rasula at that meeting in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's now move ahead in time to late March, into April of 1991. And I want you to try and recall the military exercises that you remember taking place in Sanski Most and Kljuc during that time. Do you recall that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I do recall the time. I remember those exercises. I know that it took -- these took place in 1991. But I'm not sure, but I believe that these exercises began when the war broke out in Croatia. I am not sure, but I believe it was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, these particular military exercises. You were the president of the executive board of the municipality at that time. Do you know why these military exercises were carried out in the municipality of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: These exercises -- such exercises were organised also earlier in time. I worked in the past in a body where such exercises were organised. I remember it could have been in 1982.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But addressing this particular exercise in 1991, do you know why this military exercise took place in March and April of 1991 in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, I do not claim that it was in the beginning of March or April 1991. It was either -- or it could have been June or July. And here I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: It was in order to ensure and to verify the readiness of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: All right. You're not -- you're not sure of the month in which it took place. And that's fine. It's a long time ago. Do you know who carried out this military exercise? Who was running it in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: This was organised by the Secretariat of Defence and the TO staff of the municipality. These are the two municipal bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who participated in this military exercise in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: It was under the patronage of the army. But the population participated, primarily from the municipality of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And in your view, what was the significance of this military exercise taking place during 1991 in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: These exercises were held for the broader region - Sanski Most, Kljuc, Bosanski Petrovac, and Bosanski Krupa - that's the way it should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you at the time think that there was anything unusual about this military exercise taking place in 1991, since you've stated the last one took place in 1982.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: First I had my doubts about it. It was unusual because we had this situation of war -- war situation on the territory of Yugoslavia, the war in Slovenia, the war in Croatia. In the media, we -- via the international media we could see that there was a war on the threshold of Bosnia and Herzegovina also. And in contact with the representatives of individual municipalities, Bosanski Krupa, the president of the municipality, the president of the executive board. And they refused and said they would not be participating in this exercise. Also, the area of Bosanski Petrovac ought could have been involved. I don't know what happened, but at the end it was only the area of Kljuc and Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's move ahead to the summer -- the late summer of 1991 and the series of explosions started to take place in Sanski Most. Do you recall the start of those explosions?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: First the explosions took place in two houses -- two homes of two Croatian families. In the village of Kruhari, in proximity of Sanski Most, in fact 2 kilometres from Sanski Most itself. These explosions were -- happened once a month, then every 20 days. And as April and May approached, they occurred every four or five days. And from the 20th of May to the 25th of May was the period when explosions occurred at least once a day, if not twice a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karabeg, when you refer to April and May, you're referring to April and May of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, 1992. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were Croatian families the only ethnic group that was targeted by these explosions?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No. Croatian and Bosniak. Or to put it otherwise, all others, all non-Serbs -- other non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I know again it's a long time ago. It's ten years ago. But do you recall how many buildings were targeted by explosive devices during this period from September of 1991 to May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Forty-two buildings. There were individual buildings which were targeted not once but twice. They were renewed, rebuilt, and after -- a few months later they were targeted again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What types of buildings were targeted, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: They were mostly private shops, cafes, boutiques, shops. And I also mentioned those two houses, those two homes in Kruhari.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall if any buildings belonging to Serbs were targeted with explosive devices during this period?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I heard that -- that in a cafe called Pilot, that it was targeted by an explosion. And it was owned by an inhabitant of Serbian ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown, please, Prosecutor's Exhibit 104.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I want you to think ahead in time to February of 1992 and the time of the referendum on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, the document in front of you is a proclamation to the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I see -- I recognise Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should simply like to ask whether the English version could be placed on the ELMO, because I received this list this morning and I can't find that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure it can. Thank you, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I asked you have you ever seen this document before, and you stated that you had. Where have you seen this document before and when?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: They supplied all Serb citizens with this proclamation. True that this was done in covert form, but we found it nevertheless and we were aware of this proclamation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you find this document in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, did you ever speak with any Serbs in Sanski Most about the referendum?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And what did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way. There were some of them who did vote, though a small number of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did -- please continue.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: There were some who said that they were subjected to pressure, and there were others who supported this proclamation whole-heartedly. After the referendum, then came the plebiscite of the Serb people, organised by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That plebiscite, I think, Witness, you're mistaken, was before February of 1992. But nevertheless, I have a question for you on what you've just stated. You say that some said they were subjected to pressure. Can you tell the Judges what kind of pressure you were told about and can you recall the names of any of those people that you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, you see, it was like this: There was pressure that if they don't [As interpreted] take part in the referendum, a grenade would be thrown in their apartment, their house, that they might be fired from their jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You stated that if they don't take part in the referendum. I think you meant to say if they do --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No. If they do. If they do take part in the referendum. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did they identify to you who was exerting this pressure, what individuals, what groups?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: The SDS. People from the SDS party.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I know again it's a long time ago, but do you recall the names of any of these Serbs that you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Mirko Dobrijevic, Gugo Zugic, Vuko Lepic. I can't remember any other names, but there were others too. But as I said, they were not many.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 602.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, is this a document that you signed?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, before we talk about the substance of this document, I want to speak a little bit about the procedure, about the manner in which documents such as this were signed and sealed. Now, am I right in saying that in your capacity as the president of the executive board, you signed a great many decisions and notes like this on behalf of the executive board?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Judges the process that took place when you as the president of the executive board signed one of these documents. So once the document was typed, what happened to it after that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: You see, it was like this. This was an issue discussed at the executive board, and it consisted of seven members - three Bosniaks, three citizens of Serb ethnicity, and one Croat. We voted on this. There were four votes in favour, and this document was drafted. As the president was given by the secretary of the executive board -- that is, in other words, my secretary -- this document for me to sign, which I read through and I saw that it had been entered in the register, in the protocol, and then I handed it back to the secretary to deal with it. And the procedure is that such a document is then stamped, and one copy is kept in the file to be put in the archives, and this one has -- bears my signature but no stamp. So it is a trace. It is proof that this is for the archives or the files.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think if you look very carefully, there is a -- there is a stamp on this particular copy, although it's a very poor photocopy. But nevertheless what you've said about the stamp, I want to follow up on that. Are you stating that the copy of the document that went on to the file was not stamped?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: That is how it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How many copies were generally made? Ignore this document for the moment. But generally speaking, from your recollection how many documents -- how many copies of documents were made at any one time of official decisions?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, usually -- I'm not saying that that is how it is prescribed. But unless it is required by needs -- as you see on this document, there are six addressees and the event is for the files. If not, then usually the document is copied in three copies -- there are three copies of every document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the official copy, the copy that was transmitted to other institutions or individuals, bore a stamp, did it not?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that stamp gave the document its legitimacy, its legality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just make a remark. As president of the executive board, I never stamped documents. I see that it has been entered in the protocol. I sign it. And the secretary does the rest of the procedure, takes care of the rest. And the procedure is to stamp the document and to forward it to whoever it is necessary. And then one copy is kept for the files.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the file copy is the copy which in your experience did not bear a stamp; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No, no. That is how it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. You've answered in the negative to what I've said. I just want to make it absolutely clear that the copy that was entered in the file -- wait one moment, Witness. The copy that was entered on the file did not actually have the stamp attached to it by the secretary.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: That's right. That is what I meant to say, that it is not stamped. And that is the rule, that as such it goes into the files.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about the content of this particular document. And it was one that was signed by you on the 5th of March of 1992. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the reason for this decision concern the means of taking over the executive post in the Sanski Most branch of the public auditing service. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you then state in paragraph 1: "The executive committee condemns any recourse to violence or illegal conduct to seize power, and similarly the use of force in the action carried out in the Sanski Most branch of the SDK on 28 February, 1992." Can you explain to the Judges what had taken place on the 28th of February, 1992 in the SDK.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: A forcible takeover of power by the SDS, together with its representatives in the SOS, broke into the premises of the SDK, as we call it, the payments service, and wanted by force to replace Mrs. Dobrija Sanica [phoen] who headed that institution and who locked herself up in the safe of the SDK. There was a great deal of commotion over it. There were several hundred people there. And this was thwarted, this attempt. On that very same day, I convened an extraordinary session of the executive council. We had regular meetings. But when anything like this occurred, we would convene an emergency meeting. And we tried to deal with the problem in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why did the SDS want to take over the public auditing service?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: You see, the SDK is an institution for payments transactions. Up to then -- and it was quite normal in those days -- being the capital of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, Sarajevo -- so all the resources coming from taxis were channelled to Sarajevo.
