And by taking over the SDK and replacing the person in charge, those funds would no longer go to Sarajevo but, rather, to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was this takeover, this -- as you describe it in your order, your decision -- this illegal conduct, was it ever resolved?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way: After the 6th or 7th of April, this matter was resolved in the way they wanted it to be resolved. I will make another observation. I think it was in March 1992 that three inspectors of the crime department from Sanski Most personally carried money to the army in Titova Korenica, and one of them got drunk, and the document which said that he had handed over the money and that he signed was found. And in April 1992, in one of the weekly newspapers of the Sarajevo press, this receipt was published. In this -- that is how money was collected. Actually, I don't know how it was collected, but this is what was done on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you found out that these three inspectors had carried money to the army in Titova Korenica, did you make any inquiry into that matter, as the president of the executive board?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Those were the people who were meant to carry out the investigation, in the territory of Sanski Most. They were the people who had been assigned the task of investigating the explosions that had occurred in Sanski Most municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let me ask the question of you again. And it may be that you didn't make any inquiry, in which case simply say, "No, I didn't make any inquiry." When you heard about this event --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't make any inquiry or investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I didn't carry out an investigation because they were the same people who were -- who had been given these assignments. For instance, this very document that is in front me, they were supposed to implement this decision. And in those days I didn't know that they were doing that, nor did I know that they were acting in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were the times politically difficult for you to make inquiry into this sort of event?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Indeed they were, yes. They were difficult times.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 603, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you just read that document through for me.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: "According to verified information --"

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Sorry. You don't need to read it out. If you could just read it to yourself?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if the witness could be shown also P757.2, which is a map of Sanski Most municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, what I'm interested in, in this particular document Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. is on --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's on line 7, Your Honours, of the English copy. And I'll read it because it's probably not on the same line in yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But it states: "About 500 armed civilians were noted at a meeting -- at a recent meeting of Muslim citizens in the village of Donji Kamengrad. Also present among them were members of the ZB, Green Berets, who sought that everyone who was armed launch an attack on the Serbian village of Suhace." Now, on the 6th or 7th of March, I think you recall what this event refers to -- what this report refers to. Can you explain to the Judges what you remember happening on those days and what you think this particular report is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, around about at that time two grenades were fired at the mosque in Donji Kamengrad. Around 12.00 I was sleeping at home. The phone rang, and I was called to go to Kamengrad, where a lot of people had rallied, and I was told that two grenades had been fired at the mosque in Donji Kamengrad, which had been inaugurated only a couple of months prior to that. So it was a newly built mosque. I arrived there. There were quite a lot of people. I think there may have been up to 1.000 people that were protesting. And the police was also present. The people were expressing their indignation. And about an hour later, the people dispersed and went home. The next day, the legal bodies investigated this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall if there was any damage to the mosque in Donji Kamengrad on that day as a result of these two mortar shells being fired?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No. The shells were fired into the yard of the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you look at the map next to you and just point out to the Judges the village of Donji Kamengrad. Mr. Karabeg, you need to -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I see. It's indeed marked on the map as Donji Kamengrad. Now, Witness, did you ever find out where the mortar shells that were fired towards the mosque were fired from?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Where were they fired from? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: They were fired from the direction of Suhace.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: While you were at this gathering, do you recall anybody in the crowd stating that they wanted to launch an attack on the Serbian village of Suhace?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How far is the village of Suhace from Donji Kamengrad approximately?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: The village of Suhace is about 2 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall how it was known that the mortar shells had been fired from Suhace? If you don't, simply say you don't know. But do you recall where that information came from?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, you see, I said the next day the legal authorities investigated the incident. The law enforcement bodies, that is, representatives of the police and the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that was a conclusion that they reached, was it, that the shells had been fired from Suhace, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, by them. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 604. And now we're moving ahead to late March of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you tell the Judges first of all who was Redzo Kurbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Redzo Kurbegovic is president of the municipal board of the SDA in Sanski Most. At least, that is what he was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if you could just read over this document to yourself. Have you read it? Actually, you have two documents in front of you, which --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The document that I'm interested in is the document of the 23rd of March of 1992. Do you have that document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No. I have a document dated the 12th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is -- is that Prosecutor's Exhibit 604? Could I have a look at it for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No. This is not the right document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] It's not the right document. I can see it from here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps if we agree on what document we're talking about, you could hand him your copy or Mr. Ackerman can hand his copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No. We have the right document. Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: My apologies, Witness. If you could look that document over. Now, on the 19th of March of 1992, what were you doing in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: We were there on official business.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Official government business of the municipality; correct? Or party business?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: It was an official trip on behalf of the municipality that I represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, do you know why you were stopped in this manner?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: We didn't know at the time why we were stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you were stopped, this document states, by a joint patrol of the Mrkonjic Grad public security and the JNA. Do you remember at the time being stopped by both the police and the army?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes. At the Rogolj [phoen] checkpoint, on the road from Mrkonjic towards Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were you given reasons at the time as to why you were searched and taken away for interview?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you explain how you were maltreated and questioned at the barracks in Mrkonjic Grad, as it states in this statement.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: We were taken from that checkpoint, and we were accompanied by the military. When we came to these barracks, we were taken to a room. We were questioned, maltreated - not physically though - we were searched, and all which we had on us was taken out and taken from us. Our pockets had to be emptied and turned inside out. We were maltreated, thus for about four and a half hours, and we were being told that the secretary of the SDA had been arrested -- of Celinac, I believe. And on him papers were found about the demolishing of bridges and other structures. After signing our statement, I was particularly maltreated by one of these officers, and he commented that my statement isn't proper, that it's too short, that my signature isn't correct, and that he'd really like to show him -- his own way what he thinks of me. Believe me that I tried to contact -- to establish contact. I had the numbers of two colonels with whom I had been in contact during those exercises. But I was not allowed -- in fact, one of them said, "Who cares about the colonel and you? You've got nothing to do with this." We noticed there were many soldiers there wearing red berets. Then we also surmised that this would be the barracks where the special forces are being trained and that they were in fact present there. We were a bit afraid. After four and a half hours of interrogation, there was nobody at the checkpoint so we thought that maybe they were concealed somewhere or that there would be an ambush. After that -- the next morning Mr. Redzo called and convened the municipal board and issued this statement to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the statement itself refers to an article from the AS magazine in which a statement by Mr. Kurbegovic was published. What statement, as far as you can recall, had Mr. Kurbegovic made in that magazine?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes. The weekly magazine AS. Mr. Kurbegovic gave a statement that the municipality of Sanski Most will be incorporated in the region of Banja Luka if -- only if the River Sana will start flowing in the opposite direction, namely if it changes the directions and it goes -- begins flowing upstream. When stopped at that checkpoint and when our documents were checked, the chief of police took the ID, read the name and surname of Kurbegovic Redzo. And at the time a soldier was in the container unit. He was reading the magazine AS, and at the moment -- he was reading this statement made by Redzo Kurbegovic. And when the policeman who was reading the name from the identity card of Redzo -- then the soldier said, "Who is this man who gave such statements?" And it was at that point then that we were picked up and taken away for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Cayley. Was this particular edition of the AS magazine the current edition or a past edition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, it was the current issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Current issue. Okay. It just happened to be the latest issue of the magazine, in other words, the most recent at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it ought to be like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Yes, sorry, Mr. Cayley for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I have a few more questions on this, and then if you want to take a break at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think with the indulgence of the -- how long do you expect before we take the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Well, I was going to finish with this document, and then I saw we'd go on for, I think, an hour and a half. And then if you wanted to take a break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Any time you feel like, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you say, Mr. Karabeg, that you were questioned at the military barracks. What questions were you asked, if you can recall? If you can't recall simply say "I cannot remember." But if you can, can you tell the Judges what questions you were asked.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, in concrete, they asked us what we were doing in Sarajevo, how long did we stay in Sarajevo. I believe that -- I felt free, and I told them that I was the president of the executive board of the municipality of Sanski Most, and that is why it also ended in this way it ended, namely that they let us go after four and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you say that you were made to make a statement. What were -- what did you say in that statement, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: In that statement, I stated that my name is Karabeg Mirzet, that I'm from Sanski Most, that I am the president of the executive board of the municipality of Sanski Most, that I -- that I was on a business trip, on official matters. I remember that because they -- there were complaints made in connection with that, and they insisted that I make a longer statement. And in connection with that, they also attacked that my handwriting is no good. I will just mention that because of that, that -- I won't say I was forced, but I was asked to write in Cyrillic script, but I answered that I don't know how to write in Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think if you wish, Mr. President. How long do you wish to take?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thirty minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Thank you. Thirty minutes. Thirty minutes, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cayley. You may proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, one small matter. There was a witness who was due to appear next week who for personal reasons is unable to come until later. I don't have the full details, but I'm going to get them before we break at lunchtime so I can inform the Court and the Defence of the change in the witness order.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, we left off in March of 1992. And I'd like to remain in that month for a little longer. In or about March of 1992, you saw a number of helicopters flying around Sanski Most. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you can remember, can you tell the Judges --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if the witness could be given Prosecutor's Exhibit 757.2, which is a map of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, if you can -- and again, if you can't remember, say so. Do you remember where you saw those helicopters in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if it could be placed on the ELMO. And if Mr. Karabeg could be given a pointer so that he can show the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Kruhari, Podlug.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you saw helicopters in Kruhari and Podlug. Anywhere else, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I saw them also in Dabar. They were heading to Dabar.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What sort of helicopters were they? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: These were military helicopters.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How did you know they were military helicopters?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: There were no other helicopters flying over these areas except for military helicopters.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you know at the time what they were actually doing in those villages?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, we did know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: They were bringing in weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How did you know that? How did you know they were bringing in weapons?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: We knew that they were bringing in weapons from certain -- we heard that from individual Serbs who were talking about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But you yourself never actually saw weapons being offloaded one of these helicopters?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No. No, I haven't, no I've never seen it personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How many times did you see helicopters in and around Sanski Most in these three villages?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, I saw the helicopters when they were landing in Kruhari and in Podlug. These are villages in close proximity of Sanski Most. In other words, these are almost suburbs of Sanski Most. They're -- the distance is some 2 or 3 kilometres from Sanski Most. As far as Dabar is concerned, I saw them heading in that direction of Dabar, because Dabar is much further from Sanski Most and it's also a scattered village on a broader area than Kruhari and -- of Kruhari and the other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And Kruhari, Podlug, and Dabar are all Serbian villages; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you say "military helicopters," you mean helicopters belonging to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, helicopters of the JNA. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Actually, if the map could remain there for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I want you to turn your mind to the principal political discussion that is you remember taking place in late March and early April 1992 in the municipal assembly. What was the main issue that the SDS was raising and discussing in the municipal assembly in March and April of 1992 as far as you remember?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, the main issue was the proclamation of the municipality of Sanski Most as Serbian Sanski Most, and the integration of that municipality in the region of Banja Luka. During the assembly sessions, this issue was never placed on the agenda except for the last session held on the 6th -- or the 7th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you've already confirmed to the Court that no single party had an absolute majority in the municipal assembly. Was the reason why this matter was never placed on the agenda because the SDS did not have a sufficient number of seats in the assembly to place it on the agenda?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, as far as Sanski Most integrating into the Banja Luka region, did you ever discuss this matter with any of the senior SDS members in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, I did discuss it with the president of the municipal board of SDS of Sanski Most, with Brkic [As interpreted]. And what did he say to you about the integration of Sanski Most into the Banja Luka region?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: He said that they didn't put it forward as yet but that they will and they will place it on the agenda under pressure from Banja Luka -- that is, from the pressure exerted by Krajisnik and Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, did he specifically mention those two names to you, Krajisnik and Brdjanin, as far as you can remember, that that's where the pressure was coming from in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, he did, because we were really exceptionally close. We had very good relations. There was empathy between the two of us. Don't misunderstand it. That person studied in Novi Sad, but he was from Sanski Most. And our first contacts were such that we then became friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karabeg, in the transcript it says that the president of the municipal board of the SDS of Sanski Most was Brkic. Can you give the Court the full name of this man that you're speaking about, this man with whom you had empathy.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Vlado Vrkes is the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I suggest something to you, Mr. Cayley. Could the witness be shown his statement and refer to the first page where he lists the SDS representatives and point to us whether this person that he's mentioned -- mentioning features in that list, because that would solve the spelling problem and everything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We can note on the monitor that the witness is pointing to the first person that appears in that list, namely Vlado Vrkes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I suggest for the purposes of the transcript, Your Honour, the witness is referring to page 2 of his statement of the 24th and 25th of July of 1999, and he's referring to the Bosnian version of that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you state that Mr. Vrkes told you that pressure was being exerted by the two named individuals. Did he explain to you what kind of pressure was being exerted?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, that it's high time that Sanski Most be proclaimed as Serbian Sanski Most and that it's high time that Sanski Most be integrated in the region, because it's the only municipality out of the 17 municipalities in the Bosnian Krajina area which hasn't been integrated and -- the assembly has not yet decided on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Vrkes express to you his views on this pressure being exerted upon him?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, he -- he supported that, and they were constantly asking for this. But my assumption is that this was also a conviction that maybe we would accept this and that in the assembly they would get 31 votes for this, 31-vote majority out of the 60 possible votes. Frankly speaking, we expected this question to be raised even much earlier, but it happened at the beginning of April 1992. So at a certain point also this question had to be -- this issue had to be raised on the -- placed on the agenda. And I repeat, it had to be placed on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you've already stated that the municipal assembly stopped meeting on the 6th or 7th of April of 1992. Did the municipal assembly ever vote on the issue of Sanski Most joining the Banja Luka region of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No, it did not. We set up a committee which I was a member of, in order to try to find a solution and to place this on the agenda. And this committee then -- we parted our ways and we never reconvened. This was the last session of the legally formed assembly of the municipality of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We'll come back to the discussions that you had subsequent to the final meeting of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But if the witness could now be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 608.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I do not wish you to read this entire order. What interests me are two things. First of all, the preliminary paragraph; and secondly, the first paragraph of the operative part of the order. Now, you will see that this is an order which is from the command of the 5th Corps. It is signed apparently on behalf of General Momir Talic. And you will see that in relevant part, there is a comment on the complexity of the political and security situation in Sanski Most, Prijedor, Kljuc, Mrkonjic Grad, and Sipovo, and then an order to the 10th Partisan Division -- to the 6th Partisan Brigade to pull out of a certain area and then to redeploy into the Sanski Most region. Now, the question that I have for you is: Do you recall the arrival of the 6th Partisan Brigade in Sanski Most in early April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the significance of that event, can you tell the Judges how things changed after the arrival of that brigade, whether they got better, whether they got worse.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: That is considered the date that all evil began in Sanski Most. That brigade was deployed in such a way that checkpoints were established in the town of Sanski Most and even outside it in certain villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, these checkpoints, if you can remember, what was their purpose?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, you see, at first the citizens would be stopped simply to be asked to show their IDs. All citizens of Sanski Most municipality, regardless of nationality. A few days later citizens of Bosniak and Croatian nationality or ethnicity started to be stopped, their vehicles searched in detail. There was an increase on the part of those soldiers of -- incidence of shooting and intimidation of the population with automatic weapons. And also, mistreatment in the sense of derogatory terms like balija and Ustasha. "What are you doing to us in Croatia," they would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if you the remember, who was the commander of the 6th Partisan Brigade in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Colonel Basara. I met him then, and that was when I had my first contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the members of the 6th Partisan Brigade, the soldiers of the 6th Partisan Brigade, from what part of Bosnia-Herzegovina were these soldiers recruited?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: From the municipality of Sanski Most mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How did the Serbian population react to the coming of the 6th Krajina Brigade back to Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: They were pleased and satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How did these soldiers behave in the town?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, most of the soldiers behaved in an unruly manner, in an arrogant manner. They drank a lot. What was the worst was their intimidation of the population by firing their automatic weapons into the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you yourself see soldiers who were drunk in the town of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Oh, yes. In the street. I would walk around in the streets, and they would be in the streets. I didn't, true enough, go into the coffee bars and other establishments where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see soldiers firing off their weapons into the air?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you've stated to us that there came a time when Bosniak and Croat persons started to be stopped, their vehicles searched in detail. Do you know whether searches of people of Serb ethnicity, these intensive searches were taking place at the same time?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No. I personally on a number of occasions was searched, both I and the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why were Serbs no longer searched?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, you see, at first we welcomed it. We welcomed the fact that there was no distinction made. So we've come and we will act in this way, even-handedly. But a few days later, we'll act in the way we had planned to act anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, did you meet with Colonel Basara shortly after the brigade arrived in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And why did he say the brigade had come to Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: He said that the brigade had come to Sanski Most to keep the peace and to suppress the extremists who had appeared attached to the SDS and the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did he keep to that representation, to that undertaking, Colonel Basara? Did he keep the peace and suppress the extremists?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No. But please let me add: My contacts with Basara took place only after that assembly meeting fell apart. And when the leadership of the SDS didn't want to have anything to do with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you believe Colonel Basara when you first met him that his purpose was to keep the peace in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, we didn't believe him. But the situation was such that we had no choice but to believe him and to win him over, to do what he had promised to do. And he had promised that he would establish peace in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 610.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you will see that this is a document dated the 3rd of April of 1992, apparently signed by Nedeljko Rasula, and it is a decision on the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most to become part of the Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you can see from the file number, from the BROI [phoen] number, that it is in fact document 1 of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were you aware in April of 1992 that the SDS -- that the Serbian people's Assembly in Sanski Most had made this decision?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I'm right in saying that the municipal assembly went on meeting after this decision had been taken by the Serbian people's assembly?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: You mean the legal municipal assembly of Sanski Most? No. We, as I said, on the 6th or 7th of April, we convened a meeting of the legal assembly of Sanski Most municipality which was interrupted, as I have already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you regard this decision as legal or illegal?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: All this indicates -- just a moment, please. I didn't quite understand your question. In what respect do you mean legal or illegal?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was this decision for Sanski Most to join the Autonomous Region of Krajina a lawful decision of the municipal bodies of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No. This decision was made probably by deputies of Serb ethnicity who were living in Sanski Most municipality, probably 24 of them, because as I mentioned, the municipality had 24 SDS deputies -- no, 23. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's move to the period between the 11th of April and the 19th of April of 1992. And I think I'm right in saying that discussions took place between the SDA and the SDS. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And what did those discussions concern?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, it was like this: After the assembly was -- meeting was suspended or fell apart, we sought contact so that we could continue the work of the lawful bodies, the work of the lawful assembly, the work of the lawful executive council, and the work of all the municipal bodies within the territory of Sanski Most municipality. This was what we did and the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were there discussions during this period concerning the splitting of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: There were.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges about those discussions.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Representatives of the SDS sought to have the Sanski Most municipality divided to correspond to the ethnic composition of the population, which we did not accept under any circumstances. We wanted and insisted on the municipality of Sanski Most remaining such as it was, a municipality of all three peoples inhabiting it as well as all other peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's speak a little bit about the police force in Sanski Most. What happened in respect of the police force on or about the 11th of April of 1992, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: That was when the policemen were called and they were told that they needed to sign loyalty to the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most, that they had to wear insignia of the Serbian police, and that on the building of the police, the militia as we called it in those days, a Serbian flag should be hoisted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did any non-Serbs sign the loyalty oath -- take the loyalty oath and accept this position?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No one accepted but a policeman of Croat ethnicity, one policeman, who apologised and said that he had to accept because he had been sanctioned by the police in Banja Luka and he had been sent to work in Sanski Most as a punishment. And as he was living with his family in Banja Luka, he had to commute daily between Sanski Most and Banja Luka. And that is why he accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 759, please. If you'd give that to me, I'll turn it to the right page. No. No. 7 -- it's all right. In fact, I'll give you my copy, because I have the English version. I think I've -- this is Rasula's diary, 759.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I know you don't read Cyrillic very well, and I know this document is difficult to read, but if you look to the right-hand side of that diary, there are entries from the 14th of April of 1992. First of all, do you recognise this handwriting at all?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No, I don't recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, what I want to do is to read to you what is stated in this diary about events taking place at the time and then ask you a number of questions. And I'll summarise some of it for the ease of the interpreters. But in essence -- well, the title of the meeting is "Course of action in taking over power and establishing the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most," dated 14 April 1992. And in essence, it then goes on to say, "That following intra-party agreements based on the principles based upon electorally agreed on regulations" -- it doesn't actually make much sense -- "and on the basis of electoral results dictated by political events in Yugoslavia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, a radical mode of obtaining objectives has been undertaken, a path which had to be followed by the Serbian people. And then it refers to a meeting held on the 14th of April, 1992 where three matters are decided. "That negotiations with the SDA concerning the division of the Sanski Most municipality be drawn to a conclusion; that employees of the public security service declare their loyalty to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and their acceptance of Serbian symbols and insignia; that any possibility of opposition or intervention on behalf of the adversary be thwarted." There then appears a list of names. Now, Mr. Karabeg, you were in Sanski Most at the time, but you were obviously not at this meeting. But do you recall the date on which the negotiations with your party ceased concerning the division of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: That would have been about the 13th or 14th of April, 1992, when we didn't want to discuss at all the possibility of a division of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, this document also states that "Employees of the public security service declare loyalty and wear Serbian symbols." And you've already referred to that. Were you aware at the time that this meeting had taken place that this special meeting on establishing the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most had taken place?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When was your last meeting with representatives of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: The last meeting with representatives of the SDS was held in the municipality building on the 18th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, on the 17th of April of 1992, I think you were contacted by the Muslim and Croat police officers in Sanski Most. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What did they speak to you about?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, you see, we -- this was the first time -- the first time that the SDS raised this issue was on the 11th of April, 1992. The question of the police, their loyalty, the symbols of the Serbian police, and the flag. On two occasions we requested that this matter should be decided by us, that we should be given 48 hours' time to decide, and this was accepted once and the second time as well, and then Friday came. And I was told that the policemen had been thrown out of the building of the police station because no one accepted this loyalty and that in the building, there was Rasula and Colonel Basara. When Rasula told them, "This is not the right place for you. Get lost from here." I was informed about this. I went to the building of the police station. I asked to talk to someone. I didn't see Rasula or Basara there because they had left. And I stayed there until 1.00. I was there and Redzo Kurbegovic; we were together. And I said, "My God, we asked to be given a part of the building where the Secretariat for Defence and the TO was housed. They won't give it to us. Our only solution is go to the -- is to go to the municipality building," and that is what we did. I have to point out once again that during those days, we were having talks in the police building. And while we were there, there were two military APCs with weapons who were circling round the building. When we went to the municipality building, I was informed that our policemen, that is, policemen of Bosniak and Croat ethnicity, were in the building of the fire brigade centre. I have to observe the following: In the meantime, Colonel Basara did come to see me. He spent some 10 or 15 minutes with me. To this day, I don't know why he had come, but I do know that his bodyguard and personal driver Macola [phoen] -- I don't know for what reason -- pointed his pistol here at my temple and threatened me. So they left straight away. They went to Palanka, where the brigade was based. And the policemen from the fire brigade centre, all of them, came to the municipality building.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could interrupt you there, Witness. What did Colonel Basara talk to you about during that meeting, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: It wasn't really a meeting, you see. He just dropped in the building. And as I said, I don't know to this day why he came, what he wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did he see his driver put a pistol to your head?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: We were in the same room.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did he say anything when he saw his driver put a pistol to your head?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, we've got to the position -- you've already said in your evidence where you and the police are now in the municipal building. And I want to very quickly before the end of the session today move to the 19th of April of 1992. I'm sorry. Let's go back to the 17th of April. A meeting in Tomo Delic's cafe, do you recall that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Apart from yourself, who was present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Apart from me, there was Redzo Kurbegovic, the president of the SDA; Sabic Suad; Biscevic Faik; Tunjic Anto, president of the HDZ; and I can't remember now -- there was another representative of the HDZ. I can't remember his name just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who from the SDS was present at that meeting, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: On behalf of the SDS, there was Vrkes Vlado, Boro Savanovic, and Tomo Delic. And that was in his cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was discussed at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I think it was conducted in a tolerant atmosphere. In fact, Tomo Delic treated us to drinks, and he said that we should resolve the problem and that we would continue the talks, the most probable solution would be to split up the municipality building, that half would be given to us and half to the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you arrange to meet again with them that day?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We arranged to meet at 10.00 in the evening, at 2200 hours, in the municipality building.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did that meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: That meeting did not take place, because around half past 9.00 they called me up in person --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who called you up?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Vlado and Tomo -- Tomo Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What did they say to you when they called you up?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, let me see. They in a wailing voice asked me that we should leave the municipality building because their extremists from the SOS had decided to attack the municipality. They cannot and dare not come to that meeting; and that they appealed to us to abandon the building, to leave the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How did you respond to that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Our response was that we would not leave the building under any circumstances, and we remained in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's move to the 19th of April of 1992. On this day, I'm right in saying that you were still in the municipality building; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, throughout that time. I also spent the nights there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think on the 19th of April, you got a call from Mr. Rasula; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: In concrete terms, Rasula called up Suad Sabic and informed him. It was about half past 9.00 -- that he was setting us an ultimatum, that by 10.00 we should leave and go to the park in front of the building with our hands up, lay down our weapons, and nothing would happen to us if we acted in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I fully agree. Mr. Karabeg, we have to stop here for today. Tomorrow morning we will continue. And hopefully we should be able to start with your testimony sharp at 9.00 in the morning. This morning I did send someone to explain to you the reason why you came -- you were introduced late into this courtroom. The reason was that we had a few procedural matters to discuss here. They had absolutely nothing to do with you. And please do accept our apologies for having kept you waiting in the room for more than three quarters of an hour. Thank you. Yes Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's just on the order of witnesses, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness 7.13 -- that's BT16 -- witness with protective measures is replacing Witness 7.112.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Witness 7.112 will be delayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Will replace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: After 7.76; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No. Before 7.76. The order now goes Mr. Karabeg, Mr. Begic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then I have 7.48.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. You've changed it again. This was the last that I was given -- that we were given on the 21st of May, and it was in this order: After the present witness, 7.11 --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No. This witness is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. After this witness, then there was 7.11, 7.48, 7.76, then 7.112, who is now going to be postponed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Correct. And he's going to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Replaced by 7.13.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Well, interestingly I've still got 7.76 on this list but not on this list. I'll clarify it with the staff and I'll get back to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please. It's more important for the Defence than to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Exactly. And that's why I'm saying I'll clarify it and I'll confirm it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I thank you, Mr. Cayley. As usual, you have been most cooperative. Thank you. The sitting is adjourned -- the trial is adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: at 1.47 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 28th day of May, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
